analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling off the California, Oregon, and Washington coasts.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, leaving no permanent drilling ban on the West Coast outer Continental Shelf.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Department from ever leasing any area off the coasts of California, Oregon, and Washington for oil or gas exploration, development, or production. This would make permanent the West Coast's de facto protection from offshore drilling, removing the risk of spills along a coastline that supports fishing and tourism. It was introduced by Senator Boxer with five Democratic cosponsors from West Coast states and never advanced beyond a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities in California, Oregon, and Washington, along with the people who depend on fishing, tourism, and clean beaches, would benefit from a permanent legal barrier against offshore drilling and the oil-spill risk that comes with it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: West Coast coastal communities and ocean-dependent businesses

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new section to the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act stating that the Secretary of the Interior 'shall not issue a lease for the exploration, development, or production of oil or natural gas' in any area off California, Oregon, or Washington, overriding any other provision of law [S3].

Because the prohibition is statutory, it would be permanent and could not be undone by a future administration changing its own five-year leasing plans, unlike the current practice of leaving the West Coast off each lease plan [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose the legal possibility of leasing West Coast outer Continental Shelf acreage for exploration and production, and the federal government forgoes any future lease revenue from that area.

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently forecloses domestic energy development off the West Coast, forgoing whatever oil and gas resources and associated federal lease revenues exist there, regardless of future energy conditions [S2].

Because it is written as an absolute prohibition notwithstanding any other law, it offers no flexibility for future technology or emergency circumstances; Congress would have to act again to allow any drilling [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a permanent, certain protection against oil-spill risk on the West Coast for the loss of uncertain future energy development and federal lease revenue in that area. For the coastal states whose senators sponsored it, the protection is the point; whether that is worth it nationally depends on how one weighs speculative energy resources against environmental risk.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Boxer introduced the West Coast Ocean Protection Act on January 22, 2013, with Senators Cantwell, Feinstein, Merkley, Murray, and Wyden joining as original cosponsors [S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S1].
That referral was the bill's final action; the committee held no hearing or markup, and the full Senate never voted on the bill during the 113th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies retained the possibility of future West Coast outer Continental Shelf leasing, since no statutory prohibition was enacted. West Coast communities are left relying only on each administration's discretionary choice to keep the area off its five-year leasing plans, which can change with each new president.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently prohibit oil and gas leasing off the West Coast outer Continental Shelf.

for.name: 6 of 55 Senate Democrats
for.role: Original sponsor and cosponsors (Boxer, Cantwell, Feinstein, Merkley, Murray, Wyden)
for.what_they_did: Introduced and cosponsored the bill; all six represent California, Oregon, or Washington.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats from the three affected states; no Republican ever signed on and no vote ever occurred, so opposition was expressed only through inaction in committee.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar them from any West Coast outer Continental Shelf leasing, eliminating a potential area of future operations. Its premise is that drilling off these coasts exposes coastal residents and ocean-dependent businesses to spill risk.

industries.industry: West Coast fishing and coastal tourism businesses
industries.note: These businesses depend on unpolluted coastal waters and beaches; a statutory drilling ban protects the resource they rely on. Their gain would come at the oil industry's expense.
